2. Cardinality, countability, and non-negative sums#

2.1 Cardinality and countability#

Definition 2.1.1 (Finite, infinite, and countable sets)#

A set is finite if there are and a bijection . It is infinite if it is not finite.

A set is countably infinite if there is a bijection . It is countable, or at most countable, if it is finite or countably infinite.

2.1.1 Digression on cardinality#

Definition 2.1.2 (Comparison of cardinalities)#

Two sets and have the same cardinality, written or , if there is a bijection .

Write if there is an injection . Write if there is an surjection .

Both these relations are reflexive, and transitive. One can show that the existence of an injection is equivalent to the existence of a surjection (this, I believe, uses the axiom of choice). The next theorem shows that is indeed an order relation.

Theorem (Cantor–Bernstein theorem)#

Let and be sets. If there are injections and , then there is a bijection .

The proof is outside the scope of these notes.
